title: The Two Gentlemen of Verona
author: William Shakespeare
openingChapterLabel: Act 1, Scene 1 — Verona. An open place
openingText: Valentine is leaving Verona to see the world at the Duke's court in Milan, and teases his best friend Proteus for staying at home because he is in love.
about:
The Two Gentlemen of Verona is probably one of Shakespeare's first comedies. Valentine and Proteus are best friends. Valentine travels to Milan, where he falls in love with Silvia, the Duke's daughter. Proteus stays in Verona with his beloved Julia, but his father soon sends him to Milan too, and the moment he sees Silvia he forgets both his love and his friendship.

Proteus betrays Valentine's plan to elope, gets him banished, and courts Silvia himself. Julia, disguised as a boy, follows Proteus to Milan and ends up serving as his page — even carrying his love messages to Silvia. Valentine, meanwhile, becomes the leader of a band of outlaws in the forest. The comic servants Speed and Lance, with Lance's dog Crab, mock their masters throughout.

The play ends in the forest with a sudden reconciliation that has puzzled readers for centuries. Many later Shakespeare comedies, from Twelfth Night to As You Like It, reuse its ideas: the girl disguised as a boy, the escape to the forest, friendship tested by love.

whyItMatters.title: Friendship against love
whyItMatters.body: The play asks what happens when a best friend wants the same person you do. Proteus chooses badly, and the play makes us watch every step. It is an early, raw version of a story told many times since.

whyItMatters.title: An uncomfortable ending
whyItMatters.body: The final scene is short and shocking, and readers still argue about it. It is a good test of how much a happy ending can be trusted.

whyItMatters.title: The first Shakespeare heroine in disguise
whyItMatters.body: Julia's journey as a boy is the first sketch of Viola and Rosalind. She is braver and more loyal than either gentleman.

angleCards.title: Proteus
angleCards.text: Follow Proteus's speeches when he talks himself into betrayal. How does he justify it?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to watch how Proteus argues himself into betraying his friend and his love.

angleCards.title: Julia
angleCards.text: Track what Julia sees and suffers in disguise, and how she still acts with courage.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Julia's story and see how the disguised heroine carries the play.

angleCards.title: Masters and servants
angleCards.text: Compare the lovers' speeches with Speed's and Lance's jokes about love and loyalty.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to see how the servants' comedy comments on their masters' romance.

angleCards.title: The ending
angleCards.text: Read the last scene twice. Is the reconciliation earned?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to judge whether the play's final reconciliation works.

cast.name: Valentine
cast.description: A young gentleman of Verona who goes to Milan, falls in love with Silvia, is betrayed and banished, and becomes leader of the outlaws.

cast.name: Proteus
cast.description: Valentine's best friend, in love with Julia until he meets Silvia, after which he betrays them all.

cast.name: Julia
cast.description: Proteus's love in Verona. She follows him to Milan dressed as a boy and serves as his page.

cast.name: Silvia
cast.description: Loved by Valentine, courted by Proteus and the foolish Thurio; she stays true to Valentine.

cast.name: Lance and Crab
cast.description: Proteus's servant and his ungrateful dog, whose scenes are among the play's funniest.

cast.name: The Duke of Milan
cast.description: He wants Silvia to marry Thurio and banishes Valentine when he learns of the planned elopement.
